title: Pacing pebble — microburst latency vs per-query dollar sampler (pilot notes)
body:
Summary:
This note summarizes a small pilot (pacing = 'pebble' pattern) that measures microburst behavior and the resulting p50/p90/p99 latency tradeoffs vs per-query dollar cost under three pacing configurations. The aim is to produce short, actionable collateral for infra/product on a low-effort knob that smooths spikes without materially increasing $/q for typical chat workloads.

Why this micro-experiment:
- Teams keep asking for a lightweight pacing heuristic that reduces p99 jank during short bursts (1–10s) without changing model variants.
- Full slot/tiling changes are higher-friction; pacing is a lower-risk operator-level policy.
- Need quick numbers to decide if we should add a "pebble" pacing suggestion to Optimize recommendations.

Tested configs (names below used in charts):
- steady (baseline): no pacing, default admission.
- pebble-soft: small pacing window, queue allowlist up to 40ms per request.
- pebble-hold: slightly larger pacing window, allowlist up to 120ms per request (aims to absorb 2–3 token decode spikes).

Environment / model / inputs:
- Model: open-llm/v2-13B (prod-ish reference profile), float16, sparse KV disabled.
- HW: 8xA100-like inference pool (shared), single-tenant slice per test run.
- Batching: continuous batching enabled, target batch size 8.
- Workload: synthetic session mix derived from customer chat trace A (50k sessions sampled):
  - median turn length: 16 tokens out
  - 95th turn length: 78 tokens out
  - arrival pattern: base rate 200 qps with random microbursts reaching 1200 qps for 2–8s (Poisson superimposed).
- Duration: 3 runs per config, each 30 minutes, seeded with same trace replay.

Raw ascii charts (aggregated across runs). Each chart: columns = throughput snapshot, rows = latency bucket. Throughput snapshots: steady(200qps), burst-peak(1200qps), trailing(350qps). Latencies in ms.

1) p99 spread table (ms)
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+
| Config               | steady    | burst-peak | trailing  |
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+
| steady (baseline)    | 124       | 1420       | 220       |
| pebble-soft          | 132       | 640        | 190       |
| pebble-hold          | 145       | 420        | 210       |
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+

Interpretation: pebble-soft reduces p99 at peak by ~55% vs baseline; pebble-hold further reduces p99 but increases steady-state p99 slightly (15–20 ms). For trailing tail, both improve over baseline.

2) cost-per-query (amortized $/q; rough)
Note: these are system-level estimates including GPU time and net amortized inference CPU overhead; not final pricing.
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+
| Config               | steady    | burst-peak | trailing  |
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+
| steady (baseline)    | $0.0042   | $0.0189    | $0.0061   |
| pebble-soft          | $0.0044   | $0.0114    | $0.0058   |
| pebble-hold          | $0.0047   | $0.0088    | $0.0060   |
+----------------------+-----------+------------+-----------+

Interpretation: Pacing increases steady-state $/q slightly (~5–12%) due to micro-queueing and longer time-on-gpu for queued requests, but reduces $/q substantially at the burst peak because it avoids inefficient oversubscription and expensive preemption/fallbacks.

3) simple ascii sparklines (p99 over time example run; numbers normalized to max=100 for visual)
Time (s) -> 0                     60                   120
steady        |___|_____|||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||||
pebble-soft   |___|_____|||||||||||____|||||||||____|||||||||____|||||||||
pebble-hold   |___|_____|__||||||___|||||___||||||___|||||___||||||___|||||

(visual only: pebble variants clip the burst peaks into shorter spikes)

Key takeaways:
- Pacing acts like a low-cost shock absorber: small steady-state penalty for outsized wins during microbursts.
- "Soft" offers the best steady-state/cost compromise; "hold" gives more p99 protection at the price of slightly higher baseline latency and $/q.
- For most PLG customers that care about p99 during short ramp-ups, recommend pebble-soft as a first-pass rule of thumb.

Operational notes (observed behaviors and risks):
- Under pebble-hold we observed a small increase in queueing jitter for low-latency, tiny requests (short chats). Consider a size-based allowlist (bypass pacing for <=3 token responses).
- Metrics to monitor if shipping a recommendation: percent-request-queued, queuing-latency-p50/p95, p99, slot-utilization, fallback-rate.
- Edge case: long concurrent sessions with many parallel turns (multi-tab) saw increased end-to-end session time with pebble-hold; flagging sessions with >8 concurrent turns for analysis.

Suggested collateral and next steps:
1) Create a short one-pager for Console -> "Pacing suggestions" that:
   - defines pebble-soft and pebble-hold,
   - shows the two small tables above,
   - includes toggles for allowlist based on response size.
2) Run a short A/B in staging for 48h on real customer trace B (non-synthetic) to validate steady-state penalty.
3) Add a small visual in Optimize UI: slider that shows expected p99 improvement vs expected $/q increase (use our three sample points).
4) Follow-up experiments:
   - test with quantized variants (q4) to see compounding effects,
   - evaluate with compact batching disabled to isolate pacing vs batch-size interactions.

Open questions for the team:
- What percent steady-state $/q increase is acceptable for us to recommend automatically? (product question)
- Should we provide an allowlist default (e.g., bypass for <=3 tokens) or leave it advanced? (UX + SRE)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally short-form; numbers are pilot-level and not yet audited.
- Referenced traces: customer-trace-A (anonymized) and run ids: pebble-run-20290601-a/b/c.
- If we get a green light for the one-pager, I can prepare a compact figure (SVG) for Console with the same data.

Action items (immediate):
- Marco: prep staging A/B using trace B, target start 2029-06-14.
- Asha: draft the one-pager text and UI copy, include the two tables above.
- Liam: instrument metrics for queued-percent and provide dashboards for the pilot A/B.

End of note.
